title: A curved bottleneck
objectives: Train a nonlinear autoencoder that beats PCA on curved data at the same size.

screens.title: A chord, not a curve
screens.prose: These 200 points lie along a half circle of radius 1, with a little noise: `arc(200, 0.05, seed=0)` from this level's module. Squeeze each to one number with the best line, PCA, as in l6, and rebuild it.
screens.question: Where do all the rebuilt points fall?

options.text: On one straight line across the arc, at its average height
Back on the arc, near where they started
options.why: A one-code linear rebuild lies on a line through the mean. It cannot bend round.

options.text: At the two ends of the arc
options.why: Each point lands on the line at its own place along it, not at the ends.

options.text: At the centre of the circle
options.why: The line passes through the data's mean, about 0.60 up, not the centre.

hints.text: A linear code with one number rebuilds onto a line.
The line passes through the mean of the points.

feedback.correct: They fall on a nearly horizontal line through the mean, so the error is 0.111 on these points.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What shape can a one-code linear rebuild take?

byKey.arc: You expected the rebuild to follow the curve. A linear decoder can only draw a line.

explain.text: PCA keeps roughly the left-right position and rebuilds every point near the mean height, about 0.60. The height lost along the curve is the error, 0.111 on these points.

screens.title: Bend the bottleneck
screens.prose: Now a **nonlinear autoencoder**: a tanh layer of 16 in the encoder, one code, a tanh layer of 16 in the decoder. We trained it with Adam for 1,000 steps. Switch between the two rebuilds.
screens.question: With the same one code, which rebuild follows the arc?

options.text: The tanh net's
PCA's
options.why: PCA's rebuilds sit on a straight line. Switch to the net and compare.

options.text: Both, equally
options.why: Their errors differ by a factor of about 35.

feedback.correct: The net's rebuilds lie on the arc: error 0.0031 against 0.111.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Switch the control and look again.

explain.text: A tanh decoder can bend its one-number output into a curve. The code is still one number per point, so the squeeze is as tight as PCA's.

screens.title: What PCA must lose
screens.prose: Take points spread evenly over the half circle, $(\cos t, \sin t)$ with $t$ uniform on $(0, \pi)$ and no noise. By symmetry the best line is horizontal, so PCA's error is the variance of the height, $\operatorname{Var}(\sin t) = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{4}{\pi^2}$.
screens.question: What is PCA's error here? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Variance is the mean square minus the squared mean.

byKey.half: 0.5 is $\mathbb{E}[\sin^2 t]$. Subtract the squared mean, $4/\pi^2$.
byKey.mean: That is the mean height. The error is the variance about it.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{4}{\pi^2} \approx 0.0947$; with noise of 0.05 in each coordinate it rises to about 0.0972. No line can do better on this shape, and a curved decoder can.

screens.title: The code runs along the arc
screens.prose: Colour each training point by the net's code, in four bands from the lowest quarter of codes to the highest.
screens.question: What does the one code measure?

options.text: Position along the arc, from one end to the other
The height of each point above the axis
options.why: Points at the same height on the two sides get different codes.

options.text: The distance of each point from the centre
options.why: Every point is about 1 from the centre, yet the codes span the whole range.

options.text: The noise that was added to each point
options.why: The bands follow the arc in order, which noise would not.

hints.text: Follow the colours from left to right along the arc.

feedback.correct: The code changes steadily along the arc; its rank correlation with the angle is 0.972.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the bands along the arc.

explain.text: The net found the one number that matters, position along the curve: rank correlation 0.972 with the angle. Nobody told it the data came from an angle.

screens.title: On points it never saw
screens.prose: Errors must be judged on **held-out** points: 200 new points from `arc(200, 0.05, seed=1)`. PCA's line is fitted on the training points only.
screens.question: What share of PCA's held-out error does the net leave? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Use the held-out column for both.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the net's held-out error by PCA's.

byKey.train: You used the training column. Held-out errors are the fair comparison.
byKey.inv: That is the share removed. The question asks what is left.

explain.text: On new points the net leaves about 2.7% of PCA's error. Its held-out error is no worse than its training error, so it learned the curve, not the points.

screens.title: Judged on the wrong points
screens.prose: With only 15 noisy training points, we train two nets for 4,000 steps: hidden width 4 and hidden width 64. A colleague picks the one with the lower training error.
screens.question: Which net should they use?

options.text: Width 4: its held-out error is lower
Width 64: its training error is lower
options.why: Its training error, about 0.001, is low because it bent through the 15 noisy points. On new points it does worse.

options.text: Either: both beat PCA by a wide margin
options.why: Both do beat PCA, but one is about twice as good on new points.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the held-out bars.

byKey.big: You compared training errors. The bigger net memorised the noise in 15 points.

screens.title: A full circle
screens.prose: Now 300 points round the **whole** circle, one code, the same net. Its error stays under 0.02, against PCA's 0.45. The chart shows each point's code against its angle.
screens.question: What happens to the code as the angle goes once round?

options.text: It runs smoothly round most of the circle, then jumps at one place
It rises smoothly all the way round the circle
options.why: After one turn the code would have to come back to its start. A single number cannot do that without a jump.

options.text: It repeats, so two far-apart points share one code
options.why: Points with the same code would be rebuilt the same, which the low error rules out except near the jump.

hints.text: Look for a gap in the chart.
Near an angle of about 1 radian the code leaps.

feedback.correct: It tears near an angle of about 1 radian, where the rebuilds are worst.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the chart from left to right.

explain.text: A circle has no start or end, so one number must break it somewhere: here near 1 radian. Points near the tear are rebuilt worst; two codes would remove the tear.

screens.title: What it costs
screens.prose: The net has weight tables $2 \times 16$, $16 \times 1$, $1 \times 16$ and $16 \times 2$, plus one bias per output: 16, 1, 16 and 2. PCA needs a mean and one direction: 4 numbers.
screens.question: How many parameters does the net have?

hints.text: Add the weights, then the biases.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the four weight tables and the four bias vectors.

byKey.weights: 96 counts the weights only. Add the 35 biases.
byKey.enc: 65 is the encoder alone. Add the decoder.

explain.text: The weights give 96 and the biases 35, so 131 parameters against PCA's 4. On 200 points that is affordable; on 15 it overfits, as the trap showed.

screens.title: The nonlinear autoencoder
screens.prose: A nonlinear autoencoder puts nonlinear layers on each side of the code: $$\mathbf{z} = \tanh(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2,\qquad \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \tanh(\mathbf{z}\mathbf{W}_3 + \mathbf{b}_3)\mathbf{W}_4 + \mathbf{b}_4.$$ With the same number of codes it can follow a curve that PCA can only cut across.
screens.question: When should it beat PCA at the same bottleneck?

options.text: When the data bend and there are enough points to fit the bend
Whenever it has more parameters than PCA does
options.why: On 15 points the wide net lost on new points. Parameters help only with data to fit them.

options.text: When the data lie close to a flat plane through the mean
options.why: On flat data PCA is already the best map; extra bends add nothing.

feedback.correct: Right. Curved structure and enough data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall both the arc and the 15-point trap.

explain.text: On flat data a bent decoder has nothing to follow, and on few points a big net memorises. The nonlinear net wins where the structure is curved and the data can pay for its parameters.

screens.title: The data and the comparison
screens.prose: Write the arc generator and the held-out comparison. The trained weights are in `representations-l7-ae.json` (key `params`), and `ops.tanh_ae_forward(params, X)` rebuilds rows. PCA must be fitted on the training points only.
screens.question: Write `make_arc` and `compare_with_pca`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import representations_ops_l2 as ops     # tanh_ae_forward(params, X)


def make_arc(n, noise, seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = g.uniform(0.0, np.pi, n)
    X = np.stack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)], axis=1)
    return X + noise * g.standard_normal((n, 2))


def compare_with_pca(X_tr, X_te, params):
    X_tr = np.asarray(X_tr, dtype=float)
    X_te = np.asarray(X_te, dtype=float)
    k = np.shape(params[2])[1]
    net = float(((ops.tanh_ae_forward(params, X_te) - X_te) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean())
    mu = X_tr.mean(axis=0)
    lam, V = np.linalg.eigh((X_tr - mu).T @ (X_tr - mu))
    top = V[:, ::-1][:, :k]
    T = X_te - mu
    pca = float(((T - T @ top @ top.T) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean())
    return net, pca

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step
import representations_ops_l2 as ops


def train_tanh_ae(X, hidden, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    n, d = X.shape
    params = [Tensor(p) for p in ops.init_tanh_ae(d, hidden, k, seed)]
    m = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        for p in params:
            p.zero_grad()
        loss = ((ops.tanh_ae_forward(params, X) - X) ** 2).sum() / n
        loss.backward()
        new, m, v = adam_step([p.data for p in params], [p.grad for p in params], m, v, t, lr)
        for p, q in zip(params, new):
            p.data = q
    return [p.data for p in params]

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step
import representations_ops_l2 as ops


def train_tanh_ae(X, hidden, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    n, d = X.shape
    params = [Tensor(p) for p in ops.init_tanh_ae(d, hidden, k, seed)]
    m = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        for p in params:
            p.zero_grad()
        loss = ((ops.tanh_ae_forward(params, X) - X) ** 2).sum() / n
        loss.backward()
        for p in params:
            p.data = p.data - lr * p.grad
    return [p.data for p in params]

screens.title: Curves in the yield curve
screens.prose: Daily changes in a yield curve are often compressed to level, slope and curvature with PCA (`eigen` l12). In some regimes, such as rates pinned near zero, the short end cannot fall and the curve moves along a bent path.
screens.question: What would a nonlinear autoencoder with 3 codes offer, and at what cost?

options.text: Rebuilds that follow the bend, for many more parameters and a held-out check
A better fit in every regime, with nothing extra to pay for it
options.why: On flat stretches PCA is already best, and the extra parameters must be paid for with data.

options.text: Codes that still read as level, slope and curvature, as with PCA
options.why: Nonlinear codes need not line up with PCA's named factors, so the names are lost.

options.text: Nothing, since a linear autoencoder already spans PCA
options.why: That holds for the linear one. The nonlinear one can bend where PCA cannot.

hints.text: Where can a curved decoder help?

feedback.correct: Right. It can follow the bend, if there is data enough and it wins on held-out days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh the bend against the cost.

explain.text: A curved decoder can follow a bent path that a line cuts across. It costs parameters, loses PCA's named factors, and must win on held-out days to earn its place.

ideas: On curved data PCA rebuilds onto a straight line; on the half circle its error is at least $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{4}{\pi^2} \approx 0.0947$.
A nonlinear autoencoder with tanh layers can rebuild along the curve with the same one code, and its code measures position along it.
Compare models on held-out points: a wide net on few points can memorise them, and a closed curve tears a one-number code.
summary.trap: Comparing training errors only: a big net can memorise a few points and lose on new ones.

options.why: A one-code linear decoder can only draw a line.

options.why: The line passes through the data's mean, not the circle's centre.

feedback.correct: Right. A linear rebuild with one code is a line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can a linear decoder draw?

explain.text: PCA's rebuild is the mean plus a multiple of one direction: a straight line, which cuts across any curve.
